edits.text: For exhibit display labels, use 35–50 words as the curator requested after approving a 42-word draft (Trial A). Keep detailed notes off-label. Make the first sentence and large-print species name carry the main information, since routine visitors read those and usually skip the provenance appendix. Preserve factual limits: the indoor observation was 3 of 12 buds opening; no evidence establishes the wild pollinator. A short label can still be inaccurate, as Trial C asserted an unsupported pollinator. The earlier 180–200-word planning assumption is superseded by the curator's later guidance and the unreadable 190-word Trial B. This is trial-specific guidance, not a guarantee of acceptance.

Trial A reports approval of a 42-word draft and a curator request for 35–50 words with detailed notes off-label (source 6); Trial B reports that a 190-word label was unread because it did not fit (source 7). These outcomes support revising the length guidance for display labels, but do not establish that brevity alone ensures success: Trial C was short and still failed by asserting an unsupported wild pollinator (source 7). The supplied facts report only 3 of 12 buds opened in an indoor trial and no evidence for the wild pollinator (source 4). Routine observations say visitors read the first sentence and large-print species name but usually skip the provenance appendix, without a complaint (source 5). A useful hypothesis is to prioritize the first sentence and species name, keep detailed notes off-label, and state only supported observations. These are small fictional trials and routine observations; they do not prove the revised method will always be accepted. No later Work outcomes are present in this context."}
